HSA-eligible health plans: lower premiums, tax-advantaged savings

A health savings account lets you set aside pre-tax money for medical costs and keep what you do not spend. You can only contribute if your health plan qualifies. Since 2026, far more individual plans do.

Reviewed by Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent · NPN 21370662 · Updated November 2026

Schedule an appointment Call (301) 615-8289

How an HSA works

  • Money goes in before tax. Contributions are deductible, or pre-tax through payroll.
  • It grows without tax. Interest and investment earnings are not taxed while in the account.
  • It comes out without tax when spent on qualified medical expenses.
  • It is yours. The balance rolls over every year and stays with you if you change plans or jobs.

The IRS sets the contribution limit each year, with a higher limit for family coverage and an extra catch-up amount at age 55 and older.

Which plans qualify

To contribute to an HSA you must be covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan and have no other disqualifying coverage. Starting January 1, 2026, bronze and catastrophic individual plans are treated as HSA-compatible, whether bought through the Marketplace or directly from a carrier, as long as the same plan is offered on the Marketplace. The IRS explains the change in Notice 2026-5.

That matters because bronze plans are often the lowest-premium ACA plans. Many people who bought one before could not open an HSA. Now most can.

Check before you fund it: Not every low-premium plan qualifies, and other coverage, such as a general-purpose health FSA, can make you ineligible. We confirm HSA eligibility plan by plan before you enroll.

Covering the deductible

The trade-off with a lower premium is a higher deductible. Two ways to handle it:

  • Fund the HSA with the premium you save, so the deductible money is there when you need it.
  • Add supplemental coverage that pays cash. Accident, hospital indemnity, and critical illness policies pay a set amount when a covered event happens. IRS rules generally allow these alongside an HSA, along with dental and vision.

HSAs and Medicare

Once you enroll in any part of Medicare, you can no longer contribute to an HSA, though you can keep spending what is in it. If you enroll after 65, Part A can be backdated up to six months, so stop contributions ahead of time. Our turning 65 guide covers the timing.

Who an HSA plan suits

  • Healthy individuals and families who rarely reach their deductible
  • Self-employed people who want another deduction
  • Higher earners who do not qualify for a premium subsidy
  • Anyone who wants to build a medical fund for retirement

If you take costly medications or expect a surgery, a plan with a lower deductible may cost you less overall. We run both scenarios.

Common questions

HSA-Eligible Health Plans FAQ

Can I open an HSA with a bronze plan?
Since January 1, 2026, bronze and catastrophic individual plans are treated as HSA-compatible under IRS Notice 2026-5, whether bought on or off the Marketplace. You must also have no other disqualifying coverage.
What happens to HSA money I do not spend?
It stays in your account and rolls over every year. It remains yours if you change health plans, change jobs, or retire.
Can I have an HSA and accident or hospital indemnity coverage?
Generally yes. IRS rules allow certain coverage alongside an HSA, including accident, fixed hospital indemnity, specific-illness, dental, and vision coverage.
Can I contribute to an HSA on Medicare?
No. Contributions must stop once any part of Medicare begins. You can still spend the balance on qualified medical expenses.
